---
title: "Quiz: the random walker"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Weights are affinities: $w_{pq}$ large means "similar" (a strong link), as in the graph-cut unit.

---

**Q1.** A random walker starts at pixel $p$. What number does the random walker segmentation assign to $p$, and how is the label chosen from it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Two kinds of seeds; which one does the walk reach first?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The probability that a walk from $p$, stepping to neighbours in proportion to the edge weights, reaches an object seed before a background seed. With two labels, $p$ is object if this probability exceeds 0.5; with $K$ labels it takes the label with the largest probability.
:::

---

**Q2.** Why do we never simulate random walks to compute the segmentation?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where does the walker go in its first step?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The probability at a pixel equals the weighted average of its neighbours' probabilities (condition on the first step), with 1 and 0 fixed at the seeds. That is a sparse linear system, one equation per unlabelled pixel, solved exactly. Simulation would need thousands of walks per pixel for two correct decimals.
:::

---

**Q3.** A chain: object seed, then edges with weights 1 and 1/3, then a background seed. What is the probability at the middle node?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Resistances $1/w$; the voltage drops in proportion to resistance.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Resistances 1 and 3, total 4. The voltage drops by $1/4$ across the first resistor: the middle node is at $3/4 = 0.75$. Check: $(1 \cdot 1 + \tfrac13 \cdot 0)/(1 + \tfrac13) = 0.75$.
:::

---

**Q4.** Can the random walker produce an object region that contains no object seed? Can a graph cut with a data term?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Can a weighted average exceed all of its neighbours?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The plain random walker cannot: a free pixel is an average of its neighbours, so a region above 0.5 must reach up to a node fixed at 1, an object seed (the maximum principle). A graph cut with a data term can: a bright blob far from all seeds may be cheaper as object than as background. (The random walker *with priors* can too.)
:::

---

**Q5.** With three seed labels you need only two linear systems. Why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What do the three probabilities at a pixel add up to?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
At every pixel the three probabilities sum to 1 (every walk ends at some seed). Solve for two labels; the third is 1 minus their sum.
:::

---

**Q6.** Seeds are a single click in the object and a single click in the background, both near the left edge of a large image without strong edges. Where will the boundary be, and how confident?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What decides the probability where there are no weak links?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Without edges, the walker is decided by geometry: roughly halfway between the seeds in resistance, wherever the image's true boundary is. Far from both seeds the probabilities are close to 0.5: the decision is weak, and the uncertainty map shows it. More (or longer) seed strokes help.
:::

---

**Q7.** Two regions of grey level 80 and 170 meet in a smooth ramp over 40 pixels. The walker puts the boundary in the wrong place. Why, and what fixes it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does the walker know about the grey levels inside regions?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The walker sees only edge weights. A smooth ramp has no weak link, so the boundary is set by the seed positions. Priors fix it: an intensity model from the seeds pulls each pixel towards the class its grey level suggests (an extra diagonal term λ in the same linear system).
:::

---

**Q8.** The graph cut and the random walker use the same weights $w_{pq}$ and the same seeds. In one sentence each: what does each minimise?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Hard labels vs real values.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The graph cut minimises the **sum of the weights of the cut edges** over 0/1 labellings; the random walker minimises the **sum of $w_{pq}(x_p - x_q)^2$** over real values with the seeds fixed. The first favours short boundaries (shrinking bias), the second spreads the change over weak links in proportion to resistance.
:::

---

**Q9.** *(math)* Write the random walker as a minimisation problem and derive the linear system for the unlabelled nodes.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Split the Laplacian into marked and unmarked blocks.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Minimise $\mathbf x^\top L\mathbf x$ with $\mathbf x_M$ fixed. With $L = \begin{pmatrix} L_M & B \\ B^\top & L_U\end{pmatrix}$ the energy is $\mathbf x_M^\top L_M\mathbf x_M + 2\mathbf x_U^\top B^\top\mathbf x_M + \mathbf x_U^\top L_U\mathbf x_U$; the gradient with respect to $\mathbf x_U$ is zero for $L_U\mathbf x_U = -B^\top\mathbf x_M$.
:::
